questions.stem:
Identify the part of the sentence that has a grammatical error:
(A) Neither he / (B) nor his brothers / (C) was present / (D) at the party.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Rule: 'Neither...nor' — when subjects are connected by 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. 'Brothers' (plural) is nearest → verb should be 'were', not 'was'. Corrected: 'Neither he nor his brothers were present at the party.' Trap: students default to treating 'neither...nor' as singular; the proximity rule overrides this.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) She has been / (B) waiting for / (C) you since / (D) the last three hours.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error: 'since' must be replaced by 'for.' Rule: 'since' is used with a specific point of time (since 5 o'clock, since morning); 'for' is used with a duration (for three hours, for two days). 'The last three hours' is a duration. Corrected: '...waiting for you for the last three hours.' Trap: students often confuse 'since' and 'for' — this is one of the most tested errors in SSC CGL.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) Between you / (B) and I, / (C) this plan / (D) will not work.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error: 'and I' → 'and me.' Rule: prepositions take object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them), not subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they). 'Between' is a preposition, so its objects must be in objective case: 'between you and me.' Corrected: 'Between you and me, this plan will not work.' Trap: 'and I' sounds formal but is grammatically incorrect after a preposition.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) The teacher / (B) distributed the / (C) question papers / (D) among the two students.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Error: 'among the two' → 'between the two.' Rule: 'between' is used for exactly two persons or things; 'among' is used for three or more. Since there are only two students, 'between' is correct. Corrected: '...distributed the question papers between the two students.' Trap: students who apply 'among' for any sharing situation miss this critical distinction.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) He is / (B) very superior / (C) to his / (D) fellow workers.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error: 'very superior' — the adjectives superior, inferior, junior, senior, prior, major, minor are Latin comparatives. They do NOT take 'more', 'most', 'very', or 'less' as modifiers. Use 'far', 'much', or 'greatly' instead. Corrected: 'He is far superior to his fellow workers.' Trap: 'very' is used with most adjectives, but these Latin comparative forms are exceptions.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) The reason / (B) for his failure / (C) is because / (D) he did not study.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error: 'is because' → 'is that.' Rule: 'The reason is that...' — 'reason' is followed by a noun clause introduced by 'that', not a causal clause with 'because'. Using 'because' after 'reason is' creates a redundant structure (reason already implies causation). Corrected: 'The reason for his failure is that he did not study.' Trap: 'because' sounds natural after 'is' but violates the 'reason...that' rule.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) The news of / (B) his promotion / (C) were received / (D) with great joy.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Error: 'were received' → 'was received.' Rule: 'News' is an uncountable noun that always takes a singular verb, despite appearing to be plural. Similarly: information, advice, furniture, luggage, mathematics. Corrected: 'The news of his promotion was received with great joy.' Trap: 'news' ends in 's', leading students to treat it as plural.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) Each of the / (B) students were / (C) asked to / (D) submit their work.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error: 'were' → 'was.' Rule: 'Each', 'every', 'either', 'neither', 'everyone', 'everyone' always take a singular verb regardless of the noun phrase that follows. 'Each of the students' = each individual student → singular. Corrected: 'Each of the students was asked to submit their work.' Trap: 'students' (plural) nearby makes students use plural verb 'were'; note that 'their' in part D is acceptable as a gender-neutral singular pronoun.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) He insisted / (B) to go / (C) to the party / (D) with us.
questions.explanation: B is correct. Error: 'to go' → 'on going.' Rule: 'insist' takes a gerund phrase with 'on': insist on doing something. Verbs like insist, persist, object take 'on + gerund'. Corrected: 'He insisted on going to the party with us.' Trap: 'insisted to go' sounds natural because many verbs (want, plan, decide) take 'to + infinitive'; but 'insist' is in the 'on + gerund' group along with 'succeed in', 'believe in', 'result in'.

questions.stem:
Identify the part with an error:
(A) Not only / (B) did he arrive late / (C) but also / (D) left early.
questions.explanation: D is correct. Error: 'left early' → 'he also left early' (or 'also left early' if 'he' is already understood from context — the subject must be stated in the second clause when the first clause uses inverted word order). Rule: 'Not only...but also' requires parallel structure. When 'not only' begins the sentence with inverted order ('did he arrive'), the 'but also' clause needs its own subject restored. Corrected: 'Not only did he arrive late but he also left early.' Trap: students see 'not only...but also' as a fixed pair and miss the missing subject in the second clause.
